title: Good Shepherd Gallery
subject: Criminal Law & Procedure
stem:
Lydia went to Mary’s private gallery, where a painting titled The Good Shepherd was hanging. Lydia falsely represented that she was an agent for the Good Shepherd Museum and wanted to purchase the painting for the museum. Lydia and Mary agreed on a sale price, payable 10 days later, and Mary let Lydia take the painting.

When Mary did not receive payment when due, she called the museum and learned that Lydia did not work there. Mary notified the police. When interviewed, Lydia admitted making the false representation and acquiring the painting, but she said she believed that the painting had been stolen from her by someone who worked in Mary’s gallery.

Is Lydia guilty of obtaining property by false pretenses?
call: Is Lydia guilty of obtaining property by false pretenses?

choices.A: No, because she believed that the painting belonged to her.
choices.B: No, because Mary would have sold the painting to anyone who agreed to pay the price.
choices.C: Yes, because her failure to pay when the 10 days expired by itself proves that she intended to defraud Mary when she took the painting.
choices.D: Yes, because she knowingly made a false representation on which Mary relied.

rightExplanation:
A is correct.

Gold Key: For false pretenses, false statement + reliance is not enough. The actor must have intent to defraud. A genuine belief that the specific property is hers negates that fraudulent intent.

Lydia lied and Mary relied on the lie. That makes D attractive. But the call asks whether Lydia is guilty of obtaining property by false pretenses. The load-bearing fact is Lydia’s claimed belief that the painting belonged to her. That fact defeats the intent-to-defraud layer. A answers that layer directly.

Silver Key: When one answer proves the lie-and-reliance layer and another answers the ownership-belief layer, do not stop at the lie. Name the missing mental-state axis.

c3.label: CUT B
c3.text: B answers the wrong element. Mary’s willingness to sell is not the deciding issue.

c3.label: CUT C
c3.text: C fabricates a rule: later nonpayment “by itself proves” earlier intent to defraud.

c3.label: CLASH A vs. D
c3.text: A and D fight on one axis: ownership-belief / intent-to-defraud versus false representation / reliance.

c3.label: CALL with Gold Key
c3.text: False pretenses needs intent to defraud. Claim-of-right belief blocks it. A wins.

studentScript: False pretenses. B is not the issue. C invents a by-itself-proves rule. A and D clash: belief it was hers versus lie plus reliance. Gold Key: no fraudulent intent if she genuinely believed it was hers. Pick A.

A.signal: Directly addresses the ownership-belief / fraudulent-intent axis.
A.lawyer: A is correct because a genuine belief that the specific property belonged to Lydia negates intent to defraud.

B.signal: Mary's general willingness to sell does not answer Lydia's mental state.
B.lawyer: The owner's willingness to sell does not negate false pretenses; intent to defraud is the relevant missing element.

C.signal: The words 'by itself proves' create a conclusive rule from later nonpayment.
C.lawyer: Later failure to pay may be evidence in some settings but does not by itself conclusively prove intent to defraud, especially given the claim-of-right fact.

D.signal: It proves false statement and reliance, but it does not answer the ownership-belief / fraudulent-intent fact.
D.lawyer: False pretenses also requires intent to defraud; Lydia's genuine ownership belief negates that element.

goldKeys.statement: False pretenses requires intent to defraud. A genuine belief that the specific property is yours negates that intent, even if you used a false statement to get it.
goldKeys.trigger: The actor lies to obtain property but claims she believed the property was hers.
goldKeys.unlocks: D: false representation plus reliance is not enough.
authority: Cornell Wex: false pretenses requires misrepresentation with intent to defraud.
CALCRIM 1804: theft by false pretense elements include knowing deception, intent to persuade transfer, and reliance.
CALCRIM 1863 / Penal Code 511: good-faith claim of right negates theft intent.

silverKeys.statement: Do not stop at lie plus reliance. In an A/D clash, ask which answer reaches the mental-state blocker.
silverKeys.trigger: One finalist says 'believed it was hers'; the other says 'false representation and reliance.'

remediation.title: False pretenses: missing intent gate
remediation.studentMove: Cut flanker answers, then clash A against D on intent-to-defraud.
remediation.tinyRule: Claim-of-right belief defeats intent to defraud.
remediation.trap: Picking D because the lie and reliance are obvious.
